newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA - TELECOMS - Service groups see unfair competition.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA - TELECOMS - Service groups see unfair competition.

text.p: Australian telephone service groups said they are keen to ensure that the deregulated market will guarantee fair competition and access from July next year.
The members of the Service Providers Action Network (SPAN) told Reuters they had recently spelt out their concerns to the Australian government.
In its letter, SPAN said the draft telecommunictaions deregulation bill had fundamentals flaws.

"SPAN believes that the transition arrangements in the draft Bill and Amendemants to the Trade Practices Act contain fundamental flaws that will undermine and destroy the clear aims of the proposed regime," it told the Department of the Communications and the Arts.
SPAN said the current draft could have an effect that would be contrary to the government's intention to establish an effective competitive market from July 1, 1997.
"They will result, inevitaby, in further entrenching the current duopoly in the fixed network and the triopoly in mobile services," SPAN said.

SPAN, whose members account for 15 percent of Australia's A$10 billion local/long distance fixed line telephone market, said the strong competition expected from the new carriers and service providers could be delayed by more than 12 months.
A SPAN spokesman told Reuters there was no facility to ensure that new carriers are in a position to negotiate a reasonable price for interconnection and access on July 1.

"In effect there is no motivation for Telstra to set out clear access and interconnection charges, so that new players will be able to access the viability of entering the Australian market," the spokesman said.

Australia's telecommunications market is dominated by Telstra, which has is the only carrier to have a telephone network around Australia. Rival carrier Optus Communictaions Pty Ltd is currently building its own telephone network.

Telecommunications analysts said it was unlikely that a new market entrant would build another telephone network, instead they would buy telecommunications capacity from Telstra and then resell their own telephone service.
Larry Williams chief executive officer of AAPT Telecommunications Pty Ltd (AAPT), the third largest carrier in Australia, said the current access and pricing regime is unfair.
"To have real competition in this country, you have to have everyone paying the same price, instead of some people paying a premium," Williams told Reuters in a recent interview.
Williams said AAPT had to pay higher interconnection fees to Telstra's network than its rival Optus pays Telstra.
He said he understood that Optus pays Telstra up to 3.5 cents per minute to connect to its network, while AAPT pays more than twice that amount.
"This pricing structure makes it very hard to compete long term as our cost structure is significantly higher then the other two carriers," Williams said.
The SPAN spokesman said there is nothing in the new rules to stop Telstra from continuing its current pricing strategy.

"When you are fighting a gorilla with someone as large as Telstra, who is still dominant in every market and can almost do anything that it wants to do today, what is he going to be able to do next year?," Williams said.
"If it (Telstra) isn't controlled it can kill competition very, very early and nobody is safe if there is not better controls of long term competition," he said.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
